extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics; researchers interested in foundations (category theory, set theory) and structuralism
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly survey of varieties of structuralism in the philosophy of mathematics, with focus on set-theoretic, category-theoretic, methodological and metaphysical variants and debates about categorical foundations. It summarizes positions, objections, and technical proposals relevant to assessing whether and how different systems serve as foundations for mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational system requirements (Tsementzis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A foundational system consists of three items: (i) a formal language; (ii) an axiomatic theory expressed in that language; and (iii) a rich universe of objects, described by the theory, in which all mathematical structures can be located, represented, or encoded (Tsementzis 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a diagnostic for whether a proposal (e.g., ZFC, ETCS, topos theory) counts as a foundation: ZFC clearly meets these items (first-order language, axioms, cumulative hierarchy). Candidate categorical foundations must show analogues for these three components to be considered proper foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical dependence objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellman/Feferman argument that category theory, general topos theory, etc. are not autonomous of set theory because the axiomatic specification of categories and topoi presupposes the concepts of operation, collection, and function, which need to be defined in a set theory such as ZFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a criterion for evaluating claims of autonomy: a categorical foundational proposal should either avoid presupposing set-theoretic notions or show how those notions can be given categorically without circular reliance on set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatch objection / assertoric requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellman’s 'mismatch objection': foundational systems need to be assertoric (describe a comprehensive universe with existence-claims) rather than merely schematic or algebraic; category theory (Eilenberg–Mac Lane axioms, topos axioms) is by nature schematic/structural and thus lacks the assertoric character needed for foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet this standard, a categorical foundation must be presented with axioms that make existential claims about objects (i.e., function as 'basic truths simpliciter') rather than merely serving as implicit definitions of a type of structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of the home address
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellman’s challenge: 'where do categories come from and where do they live?' — i.e., the need for existence axioms securing the actual existence of particular categories/topoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should ask whether a proposed foundation supplies an ontology or existence conditions for the mathematical objects it quantifies over; lacking this counts against its being a foundation in the assertoric sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy via categorical set theories (McLarty / ETCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: McLarty’s reply: theories such as Lawvere’s axiomatizations or ETCS present categorical axioms that are assertoric (making existential claims about categories, sets, functions) and thus can be understood as autonomous foundations logically independent from ZFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess categorical foundational proposals by whether they give assertoric axioms (e.g., ETCS characterizes sets by mapping properties) and whether they can encode ordinary mathematics without appeal to ZFC. Examples and technical details (ETCS as a function-based set theory, natural number objects) serve as positive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category theory as a unifying language, not (necessarily) a foundation (Awodey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awodey’s anti-foundationalist position: category theory should be understood as a general and unifying language for structural mathematics rather than as a (logical or ontological) foundation; categorical axioms are schematic and the aim is to sidestep foundational ontology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating categorical proposals, distinguish whether the proponent intends a foundation (assertoric, ontological claims) or a methodological/unifying framework; the criterion of success differs accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of identifying isomorphic objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Central to structuralist viewpoints: the principle of identifying isomorphic objects (i.e., treating isomorphic structures as 'the same' in relevant respects) is a key desideratum for a structuralist framework; it is motivated more naturally from a category-theoretic viewpoint than from set-theoretic constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to judge adequacy: does the framework support treating isomorphic instances as indiscernible/identical for the purposes of the theory? Lack of such support is a weakness for structuralist aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax invariance (categorical specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The categorical notion of structure is syntax invariant: specification of objects in terms of mapping properties is independent of the choice of a particular signature (choice of basic relations, functions, distinguished elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate frameworks by whether the characterization of structures depends on arbitrary syntactic choices or whether it captures invariant mapping properties; syntax invariance is a point in favor of categorical methods over standard model-theoretic/set-theoretic descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on structure-preserving mappings (morphisms and functors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Category theory focuses on mappings between mathematical objects that preserve internal structure (morphisms) and on functors between categories to compare different kinds of structures; this emphasis is a methodological desideratum for structuralism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing mathematical frameworks or comparisons between structures, check for the central role of morphisms/functors and whether they enable the comparative/structural analyses the theory promises (e.g., comparing rings, topological spaces, categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of structural properties = isomorphism-invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: A property P of an object A in a category C is structural if it remains invariant under isomorphisms in C (formally: P(A) ↔ P(f(A)) for all isomorphisms f). This is the criterion used to characterize what counts as a 'structural' property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use isomorphism-invariance as the test for whether a property is genuinely structural; it underlies arguments (e.g., Benacerraf, McLarty) about what features of mathematical objects matter for structuralist accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-down (categorical) vs bottom-up (set-theoretic) conception of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical approach characterizes mathematical objects 'top-down' by their mapping properties and relations to other objects, whereas set theory constructs objects 'bottom-up' from membership structure (e.g., the empty set), making their inner constitution explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the intended philosophical stance requires attention to inner set-theoretic constitution or whether a top-down, mapping-based characterization suffices; this affects verdicts on adequacy for structuralist aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical theorems as schematic/conditional statements (Awodey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awodey’s claim that mathematical axioms and theorems, as expressed in category theory, are schematic and of conditional (if-then) form and need not carry ontological commitments over a rich set-theoretic universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a criterion for reading the logical form of mathematics: prefer reconstructions that avoid ontological quantification over set-theoretic universes when adopting a categorical/schematic stance; contrast this with universalist structuralism which quantifies over all set-theoretic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to avoid global untyped identity for full structuralism
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection to the claim that ZFC or ETCS are fully structuralist: their languages still involve a global, untyped identity relation or analogue, which allows non-isomorphism-invariant properties; full structuralist foundations should avoid such global untyped identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a candidate foundation is 'fully structuralist', check for presence of untyped identity or other resources that permit non-structural distinctions; frameworks like Makkai’s FOLDS or Univalent Foundations are offered as closer fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural number objects (NNOs) as categorical criterion for numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In categorical set theories (e.g., ETCS), number systems can be characterized as 'natural number objects' — any two such objects are 'provably indiscernible' in the categorical theory, addressing Benacerraf-style worries about set-theoretic representations of numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the existence and uniqueness (up to provable indiscernibility) of NNOs as a test case: a categorical foundation that yields NNOs that share exactly the same properties (in the categorical language) is argued to better realize structuralist aims about numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between methodological and metaphysical structuralism
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceptual criterion: structuralist positions should be classified as methodological (about practice and language of mathematics) or metaphysical/philosophical (making ontological claims about what mathematics is). The distinction affects what counts as success for a categorical approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging categorical proposals, determine whether the aim is to offer a metaphysical foundation (requiring assertoric ontology) or a methodological/unifying framework (allowing schematic, non-ontological formulations); conflating the aims leads to category-theoretic debates about foundations.
